entries.caveats: Dyslexia differs from person to person; a group result does not predict what helps one reader. Most studies tested children or teenagers, in Spanish, Italian or English. A reader's own preferred settings deserve respect even without a measured gain; the point is that the site should not present unproven aids as help. Some people report visual discomfort that a tint relieves; that question is separate from reading skill. The statement in the mechanism that dyslexia is chiefly a difficulty with letters and sounds is recalled from memory.

entries.principle: Readers in a second language are slower, are slowed more by rare words, and gain nothing from idioms
entries.claim: Adults who read in their second language take about 20% longer per sentence and make about 21% more fixations than when they read in their first language. Rare words slow them more than they slow native readers. Idioms, which native readers process quickly, give them no advantage and slow them when the meaning is figurative. Many of them will use the browser's translation, which works only on real text in a correctly declared language.
entries.mechanism: A second-language reader has met each word fewer times, so recognition is slower for all but the commonest words. Nobody can understand an idiom word by word: a native reader retrieves it whole, and a second-language reader must first work out that the literal meaning is not intended. Translation tools and screen readers decide how to treat text from the language that the page code declares.

effects.cognitiveLoad: raises — for rare words, idioms and long sentences
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured in the cited studies
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: lowers — when a label depends on an idiom or a cultural reference (inferred, not measured)

designMoves: Prefer literal wording to idioms and sayings: 'We answer within one day', not 'We'll get back to you in no time'.
Use the commonest word for each thing and repeat it; do not vary terms for style.
Declare the language of the page in the code, and mark passages in another language.
Keep all text as real text; do not place words inside images.
Write dates, prices and units in a form that nobody can misread (see numerals-and-number-formats).
antiPatterns: A headline built on wordplay or a local saying, on a page that must explain what the business does.
Opening hours or prices inside an image.
A page with no declared language, or with the wrong one.

howToCheck.machine: Assert that the html element has a valid lang attribute that matches the detected language of the text (WCAG 3.1.1, Level A), and that passages in another language carry their own lang attribute (3.1.2, Level AA). Flag images that contain text other than a logo (1.4.5, Level AA). Flag phrases from an idiom list. For pages that the Prescription marks as serving second-language readers, run the test in word-frequency-familiar-words with a stricter cut-off, and allow at least 20% more time on any timed message (see reading-rate-and-screen-comprehension).
howToCheck.human: Translate the page with the browser into another language and read the result with a speaker of that language. Note what was lost.

evidence.strengthNote: Seen only as search summaries, except the W3C texts. Cop, Drieghe and Duyck (2015, PLOS ONE) tracked the eyes of bilingual and monolingual adults who read a whole novel of about 56,000 words: reading in the second language showed 20% longer sentence reading times, 21% more fixations, 12% shorter eye movements and 4.6% less word skipping than reading in the first language. Cop, Keuleers, Drieghe and Duyck (2015) found a considerably larger word-frequency effect in the second language. Siyanova-Chanturia, Conklin and Schmitt (2011, Second Language Research) found that native speakers read idioms faster than matched new phrases while non-native speakers did not, and that non-native speakers read figurative uses more slowly than literal ones. The participants were proficient bilingual adults; less practised readers are likely to be slower still, which these studies did not test. Four W3C texts were read: WCAG 2.2 criteria 3.1.1 Language of Page (Level A), 3.1.2 Language of Parts (Level AA), 1.4.5 Images of Text (Level AA) and 3.1.3 Unusual Words (Level AAA), which names idioms and jargon.

entries.caveats: The participants of the novel study were Dutch-English bilinguals (recalled from memory); other pairs of languages may differ. The quality of machine translation varies, and this record did not study it. A local saying can be right for a local audience; the flag asks for a decision, not for removal. The search found nothing specific on phrasal verbs such as 'set up' and 'put off', which teachers of English often name as hard.

entries.principle: 'People do not read online' is a half-truth: they choose what to read, and then often read it
entries.claim: The figures behind 'people do not read' are real and narrow. In a 1997 test, 79% of users scanned each new page and 16% read word by word. The often-quoted '20% to 28% of the words' is an estimate from the browsing logs of 25 people, not a measurement of reading. Against these, an eye-tracking study of about 600 news readers found that online readers read about 77% of the text of the stories that they chose. Scanning is how people decide what to read; it is not a refusal to read.
entries.mechanism: A visitor first samples a page to judge whether it will repay attention: headings, first sentences, numbers, the top of each block. Where the sample matches the goal, the visitor reads on, and stops when the text stops giving new information. Skimming under time pressure keeps the main ideas and loses the details.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — when a page lets the visitor decide quickly where to read
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the search did not confirm the usability figure that the existing record scanning-not-reading recalls
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the visitor finds the relevant part without reading the whole page (inferred, not measured)

designMoves: Make the first sentence of each section carry its main point, because that is the part a skimming reader keeps.
Do not cut content that a committed customer needs (how the service works, what is included, conditions); structure it so that a visitor can skip it or find it.
Put details that nobody may miss (price, deadline, exclusions) in a heading, a list or a first sentence, never only deep in a paragraph.
Do not quote '20% of the words' as a reason to remove information.
antiPatterns: Deleting useful detail because 'nobody reads'.
Long undivided text that hides the one sentence the visitor came for.
An essential condition in the middle of the last paragraph.

howToCheck.machine: Build a 'skim view' of each page: the headings, the first sentence under each heading, the list items, and all numerals with their units. Assert that the skim view contains each key fact that the Prescription lists for the page (for example the name of the service, the area served, the price or price range, the contact route, and any condition marked as essential). A program can test whether these items are present. Whether the skim view makes sense is a judgment by a model or a person, and the report must label it as such.
howToCheck.human: Give a person only the skim view and ask what the business offers and what it costs. Then give the full page and ask what they learned in addition.

evidence.strengthNote: Seen only as search summaries. Nielsen and Morkes (1997): the search quotes the original column for the figures of 79% and 16%; the widely cited 124% gain in usability for a concise, scannable and objective rewrite appeared only in a student's notes, figure not confirmed. Nielsen (2008) computed 'at most 28% of the words, 20% more likely' from data by Weinreich, Obendorf, Herder and Mayer (2008, ACM Transactions on the Web): 25 users, 59,573 page views logged in 2005, of which Nielsen analyzed 45,237, with an average page of 593 words. The estimate uses time on page and an assumed reading speed, with no eye tracking, and the article describes the users as high-end. As a precise number it is grade D. Poynter Institute EyeTrack07 (2007, about 600 readers in four markets in the United States, known here from press reports): online readers read about 77% of the text of the stories that they chose, against 62% for readers of broadsheet papers and 57% for readers of tabloids; about half of the online readers scanned and half read methodically, and both groups read about the same amount of text. Duggan and Payne (2009, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied; 2011, CHI): readers with half the time they needed kept the main ideas and lost details and inferences, and spent more time on the start of paragraphs and the top of pages; the authors model skimming as stopping when the rate of new information drops.

entries.caveats: The Poynter figure describes news stories that the reader had already chosen, in 2007; it does not describe a first visit to the site of a business. All the studies are at least fifteen years old. The existing record scanning-not-reading gives the writing advice; this record checks its numbers and adds the evidence that people read what they have chosen.

entries.principle: Adults read non-fiction at about 240 words a minute, and understand explanatory text slightly less well on a screen than on paper
entries.claim: A meta-analysis of 190 studies puts the average silent reading rate of adults in English at 238 words per minute for non-fiction and 260 for fiction; the often-quoted 300 is too high. Readers in a second language need about 20% longer. Two meta-analyses find that people understand explanatory text slightly less well on a screen than on paper, with no difference for stories. Any message that disappears by itself, and any stated reading time, should be calculated from these rates with a margin for slower readers.
entries.mechanism: Reading rate is limited by how fast the eyes take in words and the mind connects them; it varies with word length, the difficulty of the text, age and language skill. On screens, people tend to read faster and to check their understanding less, and scrolling removes the fixed positions on a page that help memory. These are the explanations that the authors offer; they are not settled.

effects.cognitiveLoad: raises — when a message disappears before a slower reader has finished it
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured in the cited analyses
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: lowers — when information vanishes and the reader cannot get it back (inferred, not measured)

designMoves: Do not make important text disappear by itself. If a message must time out, give it at least half a second per word plus one second to be noticed, and keep it visible while the pointer or the keyboard focus is on it.
State reading times at about 240 words per minute, and round up.
Give customers the facts that they must remember (terms, prices, appointment details) in a form that they can keep: a confirmation page with its own address, an email, a printable page.
Do not rely on one pass through a long scrolling page to convey a condition; repeat the condition at the point of decision.
antiPatterns: A notification of 20 words that vanishes after 3 seconds.
Rotating customer quotes or offers that change before a visitor can read them.
'2 min read' on a page of 900 words.

howToCheck.machine: For each element that hides itself after a delay (notifications, banners, rotating slides), count its words and read its delay. Fail any delay below words × 0.25 seconds, which is the time an average adult needs at 238 words per minute. Warn below 1 + words × 0.5 seconds; this margin for slower readers is a design choice of this record, not a published figure. For any stated reading time, compute words ÷ 238 minutes and flag a statement that is more than 20% lower. For pages that the Prescription marks as terms or bookings, assert that a print style sheet or a plain confirmation view exists.
howToCheck.human: Ask the slowest reader available to read each self-hiding message once, aloud. If the message vanishes first, lengthen the delay or remove the timer.

evidence.strengthNote: Seen only as search summaries, except the W3C text. The grade is A for the reading rate and A- for the screen effect, whose cause and size are less certain. Rate: Brysbaert (2019, Journal of Memory and Language) analyzed 190 studies with 18,573 participants: 238 words per minute for non-fiction and 260 for fiction in silent reading, and 183 for reading aloud (77 studies, 5,965 participants). The meta-analysis included participants under 60; a secondary source reports a decline of about 10% by the age of 70. Second language: Cop, Drieghe and Duyck (2015) found 20% longer sentence reading times. Screen and paper: Delgado, Vargas, Ackerman and Salmeron (2018, Educational Research Review) pooled 54 studies with more than 170,000 participants and found an advantage for paper of g = -0.21, a small effect, limited to explanatory text and larger when readers had to scroll. Clinton (2019, Journal of Research in Reading), using only studies with random assignment from 2008 to 2018, found g = -0.25, again not for stories. A 2021 meta-analysis reports a larger effect, so the estimate varies with the choice of studies. entries.caveats: The rates are averages for skilled adult readers of continuous English text; individual adults differ widely. A short message also needs time to be noticed, which the rate does not cover. The studies of screen and paper mostly tested students who read study texts, not customers who read a web page. The margin of half a second per word is a judgment that should be tested with real users. Criterion 2.2.1 has its own conditions for time limits, which this check does not replace.
